newsitem.title: USA: Jobless rate falls to 23-year low of 4.9 percent.
newsitem.headline: Jobless rate falls to 23-year low of 4.9 percent.

text.p: The nation's vibrant economy last month produced a worker's dream unseen in more than 23 years in which a record share of the population had jobs and the unemployment rate fell to a stunning 4.9 percent.

The April jobless rate, the lowest since December 1973, followed a 5.2 percent rate in March and was accompanied by a steady, though modest, pace of job growth but with little, if any, wage-driven inflation, the Labor Department said Friday.
"Let's face it. This is the strongest labor market we've seen in a generation," said David Wyss, director of research at DRI/McGraw-Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass.
"It's great for workers," said Wyss. "On the other hand, I'm trying to hire someone and having a hard time."
The proportion of the working-age population holding at least one job stayed at a record high 63.8 percent in April.

Despite its show of labor market tightness, the report failed to roil financial markets, which have been quick to retrench at the prospect of rising wages, which could lead to higher prices, lower corporate profits, or both.
President Clinton was quick to take credit for a jobless rate last seen when Richard Nixon occupied the White House.
"Our economy is now the strongest it's been in a generation," said Clinton. "This is a great tribute to the American people and to the validity of the new economic policy we brought here in 1993."

After the government reported earlier this week that the economy grew at a nine-year high 5.6 percent annual rate in the first quarter, many economists were convinced that Federal Reserve policy-makers would again raise interest rates later this month. They said the jobless rate bolstered their beliefs.
The central bank raised short-term interest rates by a quarter-point March 25 in an effort to slow the current economic expansion to what policy-makers believe is a more sustainable pace of growth.

The report, the government's first look at the health of the economy in April, showed the pace of job creation was fairly modest, lower than expected and well below the 221,000-per-month pace of the past 12 months.
The department's survey of businesses found that 142,000 non-farm jobs were added to payrolls in April, little changed from a revised 139,000 created in March.

Separately, the Conference Board reported the index of leading indicators, a key economic forecasting gauge, rose a scant 0.1 percent in March, signaling a possible slowdown ahead in the economy's recent rapid pace.
The index, which is designed to forecast economic activity six to 12 months ahead, rose 0.5 percent in February and 0.3 percent in January.

"I think that we're looking at a really robust economy, although one growing at a slower pace than we had in the first quarter," said economist Richard Berner, executive vice president of Mellon Corp. in Pittsburgh.

Despite the job market tightness, workers' average hourly wages fell by 1 cent in April to $12.14, after gaining 5 cents in March, the department said. But over the past 12 months, wages rose 3.6 percent, a faster rate than a year ago.

Economist Tom Palley of the 78-union AFL-CIO said that the higher hourly pay partly reflects overtime work for which workers receive higher pay, while a rise in average weekly earnings reflects the fact that 6.3 percent of workers hold more than one job, up from 5.8 percent in March.

"Yes, we're succeeding in generating jobs and, yes, we're succeeding in generating profits, but there's still not the wage growth for working families," said Palley. "The Fed should not respond to these numbers as inflationary."

The number of idle workers fell by 430,000 to 6.7 million and the number of job holders rose 209,000 to 129.4 million, the department said in its household survey. The total civilian labor force, which includes all job holders and job seekers, fell by 221,000 to 136.1 million in April, though it has grown by more than 1 million since the beginning of the year.
Last month's job growth occurred in a variety of service-type industries, including retail trade, health services, engineering and management, finance, insurance, real estate and government work.

The number of weather-sensitive construction jobs fell by 44,000 in April, while the manufacturing sector lost 14,000 jobs, in part because of strikes and plant shutdowns in the automobile industry, the department said.

But factories were operating in high gear last month as overtime hours rose six minutes to a record-high five hours per week, while the work week rose by 6 minutes to 42.2 hours, matching a post-World War II high.
